topic-000-characterizing-and-learning-eq.evolution: The collection spans early causal-modeling work from 1987 onward. Recent representatives emphasize conditional effects under graph uncertainty, partial counterfactual identification, and testable adjustments with limited structural knowledge. The 2026 derivation-graph work organizes equivalent causal expressions to support more efficient estimation.
openQuestions: How can identification procedures communicate sensitivity to uncertain structural assumptions?
Which limited experiments most effectively narrow an unresolved causal query?
topic-000-characterizing-and-learning-eq.overview: Causal identification asks whether available data and assumptions determine the effect of an intervention or a counterfactual outcome. These papers study situations where the full causal graph is unknown, different datasets observe different variables, or only bounds on an answer are possible. Graphical equivalence, conditional independence, and do-calculus provide ways to distinguish what is identifiable from what remains ambiguous.
topic-000-characterizing-and-learning-eq.title: Causal Identification with Incomplete Knowledge
topic-000-characterizing-and-learning-eq.whyItMatters: A predictive association alone cannot justify a policy intervention. Identification tells analysts which additional assumptions or experiments are needed before estimating an effect, and can expose several valid estimators for the same quantity.

topic-001-a-fast-post-training-pruning-f.evolution: Early representatives address network and rule pruning in the 1990s. Later papers integrate pruning into training and examine lottery-ticket subnetworks. Recent work targets deployment-specific structures, including vision-language-action models and interacting experts in mixture-of-experts language models, with layerwise subset-selection guarantees in the provided 2026 evidence.
openQuestions: When does a pruning criterion predict real hardware speed rather than parameter count alone?
How can pruning preserve rare capabilities that average benchmark scores miss?
topic-001-a-fast-post-training-pruning-f.overview: Pruning removes weights, units, or entire experts while trying to retain a model’s useful behavior. The cluster includes optimization-based sparsification, methods that allocate sparsity across layers, and searches for small subnetworks that can train successfully. A recurring distinction is between making a model numerically sparse and producing a structure that actually reduces deployment cost.
topic-001-a-fast-post-training-pruning-f.title: Neural Network Pruning and Sparse Subnetworks
topic-001-a-fast-post-training-pruning-f.whyItMatters: Reducing stored parameters and computation can make capable models usable on limited hardware. Preserving accuracy requires accounting for interactions among components, since independently unimportant units may still contribute collectively.

topic-002-boldsymbol-lambda-orthogonalit.evolution: The earlier examples include supervised embeddings and structured latent spaces around 2010. More recent work explores semantic translation and representation alignment across models. The 2026 papers extend this perspective to layerwise subspace selection and contrastive alignment between datasets and neural-network weights, illustrating several distinct uses of geometry rather than a single lineage.
openQuestions: Which geometric properties predict transfer before downstream labels are available?
How can alignment preserve meaningful differences rather than erase them?
topic-002-boldsymbol-lambda-orthogonalit.overview: Learned representations can carry useful information in different layers, modalities, or even model-weight spaces. This topic studies how to select, reshape, and align those representations so meaningful distinctions remain accessible. Representative methods use perceptual similarity, contrastive objectives, spectral structure, and geometric constraints to separate task-relevant information from nuisance variation.
topic-002-boldsymbol-lambda-orthogonalit.title: Representation Geometry and Semantic Alignment
topic-002-boldsymbol-lambda-orthogonalit.whyItMatters: A strong pretrained model does not guarantee that its final embedding is the best representation for a new task. Understanding geometry can improve transfer, cross-model comparison, and the construction of reusable model or dataset descriptions.

topic-003-a-convergence-theory-for-svgd-.evolution: Representatives move from mirror-descent aggregation and oracle lower bounds in the 2000s toward sharper nonconvex and heavy-tail analyses. Recent examples examine constant-step stationary behavior and weakly convex objectives. A 2026 shuffling study also connects statistical convergence with memory-transfer costs, showing that data access can matter alongside iteration counts.
openQuestions: Can adaptive methods attain strong tail guarantees without knowing the noise distribution?
How should optimization complexity jointly account for gradient queries and data movement?
topic-003-a-convergence-theory-for-svgd-.overview: Stochastic optimizers learn from noisy gradient estimates, so convergence depends on step sizes, noise tails, objective geometry, and data access. This cluster develops upper and lower complexity bounds alongside practical estimators and update rules. Heavy-tailed noise, biased gradients, nonconvex objectives, and minimax problems test where familiar SGD intuitions remain valid.
topic-003-a-convergence-theory-for-svgd-.title: Stochastic Optimization Guarantees and Robustness
topic-003-a-convergence-theory-for-svgd-.whyItMatters: Reliable optimization requires more than average progress on a favorable benchmark. High-probability guarantees and lower bounds clarify which failures are preventable and which reflect fundamental limits imposed by noise or available information.

topic-004-3d-vla-a-3d-vision-language-ac.evolution: The collection begins with language-perception grounding and compositional robot tasks, then includes demonstration-based synthesis. The 2023–2025 representatives emphasize multimodal foundation agents and comprehensive navigation or manipulation evaluation. Recent work broadens planning tests to realistic interfaces and tightly coupled constraints, while new vision-language-action recipes target the bridge from perception to control.
openQuestions: How can agents detect that their understanding no longer matches execution progress?
Which evaluations distinguish visual comprehension from robust long-horizon control?
topic-004-3d-vla-a-3d-vision-language-ac.overview: Grounded agents must connect visual observations and language instructions to executable actions. The representatives cover navigation, robotic manipulation, latent planning, and evaluation of embodied decision-making. They distinguish understanding a scene or instruction from tracking progress and acting successfully over a sequence of changing observations.
topic-004-3d-vla-a-3d-vision-language-ac.title: Vision-Language Agents for Grounded Planning
topic-004-3d-vla-a-3d-vision-language-ac.whyItMatters: Strong answers to visual questions do not automatically translate into reliable control. Benchmarks that test low-level actions, temporal understanding, and interacting constraints reveal gaps hidden by high-level language competence.

topic-005-a-contrastive-divergence-for-c.evolution: Early representatives investigate response corrections and contrastive divergence. Later work bridges sampling with variational approximations and develops semi-implicit or mixture families. The 2020–2026 evidence increasingly analyzes black-box optimization itself, including stopping rules, proximal parameterizations, and how second-order Price gradients explain apparent differences between parameter-space and Wasserstein approaches.
openQuestions: Can diagnostics distinguish a poor variational family from incomplete optimization?
When do second-order gradient estimators repay their additional computational cost?
topic-005-a-contrastive-divergence-for-c.overview: Variational inference approximates an intractable posterior by optimizing a simpler distribution. Its accuracy depends both on the chosen family and divergence and on whether noisy optimization reaches a good solution. These papers examine richer approximations, annealing, sampling connections, gradient estimators, and convergence diagnostics for that coupled problem.
topic-005-a-contrastive-divergence-for-c.title: Variational Inference and Posterior Optimization
topic-005-a-contrastive-divergence-for-c.whyItMatters: A flexible approximation can still give misleading uncertainty if optimization fails. Separating approximation error from optimization error helps users judge posterior results and choose procedures that are computationally practical without silently becoming unreliable.

topic-006-a-boolean-task-algebra-for-rei.evolution: The collection spans abstraction and tactical planning from 1989 to modern learned planners. Representatives from 2019–2024 combine policy learning, curiosity, graphs, and reachability-aware latent states. Recent examples extend planning design to language agents and analyze diffusion guidance through stochastic control, including probabilistic constraint-satisfaction guarantees.
openQuestions: How can a learned abstraction preserve reachability under changing dynamics?
Can planning guarantees remain useful when the world model is imperfect?
topic-006-a-boolean-task-algebra-for-rei.overview: Planning over many steps becomes easier when observations are compressed into states that preserve reachability and useful subgoals. This cluster joins goal-conditioned policies, exploration, replay-buffer search, and latent world models. The common challenge is reducing the search over action sequences without discarding the structure needed to reach a new goal.
topic-006-a-boolean-task-algebra-for-rei.title: Learned Representations for Long-Horizon Planning
topic-006-a-boolean-task-algebra-for-rei.whyItMatters: A compact visual embedding may be excellent for recognition yet misleading for planning if nearby points cannot reach one another. Representations and exploration strategies must therefore reflect controllable transitions, not just perceptual similarity.

topic-007-high-performance-zero-memory-o.evolution: Early examples concern specialized processors and GPU-based learning. Later work explores binary weights, compressed activations, and combinations of memory-saving techniques. Recent representatives include structure-preserving compression and implicit visual generators whose inference iteration count can be adjusted, reflecting attention to concrete quality–resource tradeoffs across architectures.
openQuestions: Which efficiency gains transfer across devices and batch sizes?
How can compression preserve per-example behavior, not just aggregate accuracy?
topic-007-high-performance-zero-memory-o.overview: Practical neural-network efficiency depends on memory movement, activation storage, operator structure, and hardware utilization as well as arithmetic count. This cluster includes compression, low-precision computation, offloading, rematerialization, and architectures with adjustable computation. Representative methods often preserve learned behavior while changing how the computation is organized or stored.
topic-007-high-performance-zero-memory-o.title: Hardware-Efficient Neural Computation
topic-007-high-performance-zero-memory-o.whyItMatters: A theoretically small network can run slowly if its operators use the device poorly. Measuring throughput and memory alongside predictive quality helps distinguish deployable improvements from reductions that exist only in abstract model statistics.
